sysd-found-031.title: The network layer: getting packets across networks
sysd-found-031.text: A sender only supplies the message and a destination address, and the network finds the way. That is the network layer's job: moving packets from one node to another across different networks, routing through intermediate nodes where needed. If a message is too large for the data link layer between two nodes, the network may split it into fragments. It sends them independently and reassembles them at another node. Delivery is not necessarily reliable, since a protocol may, but need not, report errors or provide reliable delivery. If the two devices are on the same network, the network layer is unnecessary.

sysd-found-153.title: ICMP: how the network reports its own errors
sysd-found-153.text: When a packet cannot get through, ICMP is how the network says so. The Internet Control Message Protocol is a supporting protocol that routers and other network devices use to send error messages and operational information about IP communication. It reports problems such as an unavailable service or an unreachable host or router. The errors go to the source IP address of the packet that caused them. Unlike TCP and UDP, ICMP does not normally carry data between systems or serve end-user applications, and an ICMP packet has no port number. Its messages travel inside IPv4 packets, and IPv6 uses a separate ICMPv6. Each forwarding router decrements the packet's TTL, explained in {{ref:sysd-found-203}}. At 0 the packet is discarded and an ICMP time exceeded message goes to the source. Ping uses echo request and echo reply. Traceroute sends datagrams with increasing TTL values and reads the time exceeded and destination unreachable messages to find each router on the path. Destination unreachable is also sent when a packet must be fragmented but carries the don't-fragment flag, which {{ref:sysd-found-150}} relies on.

sysd-found-026.title: Choosing TCP or UDP: completeness or speed
sysd-found-026.text: The choice comes down to one question: is late data worse than lost data? Use TCP when data must arrive complete and in order, and use UDP when the lowest latency matters more than losing some data. TCP has built-in error checking and guarantees that data is delivered in the order it was sent, which suits still images, data files and web pages. Its feedback mechanisms make it reliable but add overhead, using more of the available network bandwidth. UDP has no overhead for opening, maintaining or terminating a connection, and it sends data continuously whether or not the recipient receives it. It is faster, simpler and more efficient than TCP, but only TCP can retransmit lost packets. Typical TCP uses are web traffic, mail with SMTP and POP, and FTP. Typical UDP uses are video streaming, DNS and VoIP, and UDP is largely preferred for real-time communication such as broadcast or multicast transmission.

sysd-found-145.title: NAT traversal: reaching a peer behind another NAT
sysd-found-145.text: Two peers that both sit behind NAT devices cannot simply call each other. NAT traversal is the set of techniques, such as port forwarding and TCP hole punching, that lets them communicate. VoIP, videoconferencing and other applications that connect users directly must use them to work. STUN was specified to let a client find its external address and the type of mapping its NAT uses. TCP hole punching, the most popular TCP technique, needs the NAT to preserve ports for outgoing connections. UDP needs no such preservation, because many UDP communications can share one source port.

sysd-found-164.title: Delayed ACKs: acknowledging less often
sysd-found-164.text: A receiver does not have to acknowledge every segment. With a delayed ACK it sends fewer than one acknowledgment per data segment received, which saves effort in both the network and the hosts. A TCP endpoint should delay ACKs but never excessively: the delay must be less than 0.5 seconds. Excessive delays disturb round-trip timing and packet clocking. So out-of-order segments, segments above a gap and segments that fill a gap should be acknowledged immediately, to speed loss recovery. Combined with {{ref:sysd-found-014}}, both on by default in common operating systems, delayed ACKs can badly hurt request-response applications. Many applications simply disable Nagle with a socket option.

sysd-found-165.title: Silly window syndrome: the tiny-window trap
sysd-found-165.text: TCP can fall into a stable pattern of small incremental window movements that leaves it performing extremely poorly. Both sender and receiver must avoid it. Nagle's algorithm curbs tiny segments from small data increments, and silly window avoidance curbs those from a window edge that advances in small steps. The receiver moves its right window edge only when the freed space reaches the smaller of a recommended half of its buffer and the effective send MSS. The sender cannot see that buffer, so it estimates it as the largest window seen. An override timeout of 0.1 - 1.0 seconds forces data out, so a wrong estimate cannot deadlock.

sysd-found-160.title: Half-close: stop sending but keep listening
sysd-found-160.text: Hanging up a TCP connection can happen in halves. Because TCP closes the two directions independently, an endpoint can stop sending while it keeps receiving. CLOSE means 'I have no more data to send', and TCP treats it as one-directional. The closing user can keep receiving until the remote peer has closed too. An endpoint that receives a FIN acknowledges it but does not send its own FIN until its user also closes. A host may instead implement a half-duplex close, in which the application cannot keep reading after CLOSE.

sysd-found-163.title: TCP keep-alive: checking an idle peer is still there
sysd-found-163.text: TCP has no built-in way to tell whether a peer is still alive. A keep-alive sends a probe on an idle connection to check. Keep-alives are optional and not universally accepted. A connection is idle when no segments have arrived for a long time and nothing new or unacknowledged is waiting to be sent. Keep-alives must default to off, with a per-connection switch. A probe goes out only after a configurable interval of silence, which must default to no less than two hours. One unanswered probe is not proof that the connection is dead, because ACK segments without data are not reliably transmitted.

sysd-found-159.title: TCP reset: telling a peer the connection does not exist
sysd-found-159.text: A host that receives a segment for a connection it knows nothing about answers with a reset. A reset (RST) segment tells a TCP peer that a segment does not belong to a live connection. The receiver then ignores it or aborts the connection. A RST is sent whenever a segment arrives that apparently is not meant for the current connection, such as a SYN that matches no existing connection. A half-open connection exists when one peer closed, aborted or lost its state without the other knowing. It is reset automatically when either side attempts to send data, because the peer with no connection answers with a reset.

sysd-found-167.title: What a TCP header carries
sysd-found-167.text: Every TCP segment starts with a header, and its fields are the protocol in miniature. The header follows the IP header and carries ports, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, flags, window and checksum. The ports are 16 bits each. The sequence number is 32 bits, and so is the acknowledgment number, which is always sent once a connection is established. The control bits, also called flags, are CWR, ECE, URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN and FIN. The checksum is never optional: the sender must generate it and the receiver must check it. It covers a pseudo-header of IP information, which protects the connection against misrouted segments.

sysd-found-158.title: TIME-WAIT: why a closed connection lingers
sysd-found-158.text: The endpoint that closes a TCP connection first cannot walk away at once. It must linger in TIME-WAIT for twice the Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL), which the specification takes to be 2 minutes. This limits the rate of connection reuse. Segments from an earlier incarnation of a connection, an earlier use of the same connection, must not be confused with the new one. A host in TIME-WAIT may accept a new SYN from the remote endpoint to reopen the connection directly. A timestamp-based algorithm that shortens TIME-WAIT supports higher connection establishment rates on busy servers.

sysd-found-166.title: Zero-window probing: knocking on a closed window
sysd-found-166.text: A receiver's window can stay at zero, and the sender must keep checking. Zero-window probing is how it does that, so the reopening of the window is reliably reported. Even at zero, the sender must regularly transmit at least one octet of new data, or retransmit, to probe the window. The first probe should be sent once a zero window has lasted the retransmission timeout. The interval between probes should increase exponentially. A receiver may keep its window closed indefinitely, as in the 'printer ran out of paper' case. The sender must then keep the connection open while the receiver keeps acknowledging probes.

sysd-found-150.title: Path MTU Discovery: finding the smallest hop
sysd-found-150.text: Some connections work for small messages and stall once a host sends a large block, which is how a failed Path MTU Discovery shows itself. The path MTU is the smallest MTU of any hop between source and destination, the largest packet that crosses the path without fragmentation. To find it, the sender sets the DF (don't fragment) bit. A device with a smaller MTU drops the packet and returns an ICMP Datagram Too Big message giving its MTU. The sender lowers its estimate and repeats until packets fit. Networks that drop ICMP traffic break discovery. Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery is more robust to ICMP filtering.

sysd-found-151.title: Reno, CUBIC and BBR: different ways to react to congestion
sysd-found-151.text: Tahoe and Reno both treat a retransmission timeout and three duplicate ACKs as loss. On duplicate ACKs, Tahoe drops the window to 1 MSS and restarts slow start, while Reno halves it and enters fast recovery. CUBIC makes the window a cubic function of time since the last congestion event, and it has been the Linux default since kernel 2.6.19. BBR (Google, 2016) is not loss-based: it builds a network model from the maximum bandwidth and round-trip time delivered. Its fairness in version 1 is disputed. Google's presentation shows it coexisting with CUBIC, while researchers found that it can take the link from a CUBIC flow.
